prerequisites: Completion of the second study section, requiring at least 42 ECTS points from the first study section.
Solid knowledge and practical experience with at least one procedural, one object-oriented, and one logical programming language (e.g., PROLOG).
Knowledge of functional programming is advantageous.
Proficient use of grammars for context-free languages.

learning_outcomes.text: Students are able to distinguish essential programming paradigms and name their differences, advantages, and disadvantages.
Students are able to recognize the benefits of higher-order programming and apply them to suitable problem statements.
Students are able to explain the difference between pure and impure functional programming languages.
Students are able to explain the difference between typed and untyped programming languages.
Students are able to understand the advantageous influence of type information on code optimization.
Students are able to explain the connection between functional languages and the underlying Lambda Calculus.
Students are able to describe the difference between lazy and eager evaluation strategies and apply the adequate strategy depending on the problem.
Students are able to form simple equation chains in untyped Lambda Calculus to demonstrate different reduction strategies.
Students are able to create programs in the strongly typed functional language Haskell.
Students are able to implement parsers for context-free languages using monadic higher-order parser combinators in Haskell.

syllabus_topics: Overview of common programming paradigms: procedural, object-oriented, functional, logical programming
Introduction to functional programming with Haskell
Typed functional languages: Haskell, Standard ML, Scala
Realization of Lambda Calculus constructs in conventional languages like Java and Python
Implementation of parsers using monadic parser combinators
assessment_rules: The examination consists of a 90-minute written exam.
